steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Breast Diseases focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.dosing: Standard clinical care protocol under medical supervision.
drug_classes.pearls: Establish baseline clinical parameters and educate patient on trigger avoidance and early warning signs.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Dose optimization and complementary therapeutic escalation.
drug_classes.dosing: Titrate to target clinical biomarker thresholds under specialist guidance.
drug_classes.pearls: Evaluate patient compliance and consider secondary causes of treatment resistance.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Breast Diseases require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Breast Diseases.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: GFR increases by 50% in normal pregnancy; adjust renal eliminated medications accordingly.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Screen for intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy when pruritus occurs in 2nd/3rd trimesters.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Strictly utilize FDA Category A/B or well-characterized safe pregnancy registry medications.
special_populations.elderly: For postmenopausal hormone therapy, use lowest effective dose for shortest duration; transdermal preferred.

style_3_monograph.summary: What are breast diseases? Breast diseases include various conditions and changes in your breast. Most women experience breast changes at some time. Your age, hormone levels, and medicines you take may cause lumps, bumps, and discharges of fluids that are not breast milk. Although many women fear cancer , most breast changes are benign, meaning they are not cancer. These breast changes are known as benign breast disease. See your health care provider if you have a breast lump, pain, discharge, or skin irritation. Minor and serious breast problems often have similar symptoms and may need treatment. Common breast changes and conditions can include: Fibrocystic breast changes can include lumpiness, thickening, and swelling, often just before your period . Your breasts may feel painful, swollen, or tender. Cysts are fluid-filled lumps that may be tender. Fibroadenomas are solid, round, rubbery lumps that easily move when pushed, occurring most in younger women. Intraductal papillomas are wart-like benign tumors that grow in the milk duct of the breast. Blocked milk ducts. Milk production when you're not breastfeeding. What are the symptoms of breast disease? Symptoms depend on the type of breast disease. Benign breast diseases may not have any symptoms, or they could include: A lump or firm feeling in your breast or under your arm A change in the size or shape of your breast Nipple discharge Skin changes such as itching, redness or darkening, dimples, scaling, or puckering on your breast or nipple Painful, swollen, or tender breasts See your provider if you're noticing any of these symptoms or other unusual changes. Some symptoms may be warning signs or symptoms of breast cancer. How are breast diseases diagnosed? Some breast changes may be felt or seen. You may notice a change in your breast, or your provider may notice it during a clinical breast exam . Other breast changes may only be found during a screening mammogram or other imaging tests such as an MRI or ultrasound. Your provider may also recommend a breast biopsy to check a suspicious change in your breast. What are the treatments for breast disease? Some benign breast changes may increase your risk of breast cancer in the future and may need treatment now. Treatment depends on the type of breast disease that you have. Some breast changes may go away without treatment, while others may require monitoring, biopsy , or surgery. NIH: National Cancer Institute
